sm: Host Kato Del opens Potomac Watch with his Wall Street Journal editorial board colleague Elliot Kaufman, discussing the Republican losses in this week's elections. Vice President J.D. Vance posted that the war in Iran was the reason Republicans lost, including the Senate. Both hosts say the war was one reason, mainly through gas prices, but not the only one. Elliot points to exit polls where voters named corruption and cost of living as top concerns, notes Trump's economic approval was already at Biden levels before the war because of tariffs, and says more than fifty-five percent of voters wanted the same or a more active US role in the world. He suggests Vance has political reasons, including a possible 2028 run, to court the part of the base that wants out of the Middle East.

They question why Vance listed changing the US relationship with Israel as a cause of the defeat, since exit polls show foreign policy was the top issue for only four percent of voters. Elliot says it only makes sense if you accept the view, voiced by Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, that Netanyahu pulled Trump into the war, which he calls strange for Trump's own vice president to indulge. After a short ad for the Journal's Free Expression newsletter, they play Trump's remarks, in which he says he knew the war would have an impact but that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon. Elliot says Trump told newspapers he would do it again. He argues Trump never sold the war because he expected a quick one, citing his promises of four weeks and then four to six weeks, and the examples of Venezuela and the twelve-day war, so he assumed he needed no Congress, allies or public buy-in.

Elliot says that once the war dragged on, the administration pulled back instead of escalating. It accepted a ceasefire that wasn't really one and then a memorandum of understanding promising Iran sanctions relief, which Iran exploited to claim control of the Strait of Hormuz. By the time the US imposed a blockade and restored traffic, the war already looked aimless and unwinnable to most Americans. Kato adds that the April ceasefire was premature and recalls the administration's argument that Iran was mass-producing missiles to shield its nuclear program. Elliot agrees there is strategic logic there but says Trump never made the case, and Democrats' line that this was a war of choice raising gas prices succeeded partly because the administration saw a generational opportunity. He adds that air strikes have struggled against underground missile cities, and that special forces raids would need public support that was never built. After a break, Kato turns back to Vance's post and his known opposition to the war.

Kato asks whether Vance can stay in his role, since he has been leading negotiations with Iran. Elliot says credible negotiation depends on threatening force, and Vance is no longer a credible messenger because he has said publicly that his party needs out. He argues this undermines Trump's position just as the US was strengthening, with the Navy restoring Hormuz traffic and more oil leaving the region than before the war. They also note that Democrat Ro Khanna proposed a funding ban on military action in Iran. Elliot says the US should think in terms of objectives rather than escalate to deescalate, which Iran sees through. If the aim is the nuclear program, two assets remain untouched, the deep enrichment site at Pickaxe Mountain and the highly enriched uranium buried under the Esfahan complex.

Elliot says reaching those two sites would likely take a risky special forces operation. If the aim is toppling the regime, the options are a massive military blitz or going long with a sustained naval blockade that cuts off Iran's trade sector by sector. He thinks a short burst of strikes meant to win an exit is least likely to work. On internal fallout, he says he would not want Admiral Brad Cooper to be blamed, and that Pete Hegseth could be the fall guy even though he was not that involved. Factions disagree between taking whatever deal is available, which would effectively hand Iran control of Hormuz, and holding firm. His lessons for Republicans are not to start a war without public buy-in and not to wrap it up prematurely, and to avoid concluding that a president can never win public support for sustained sacrifice. He warns that the president's week-to-week will-he-won't-he approach undermined credibility with both voters and Iran, and that a narrow reading of the loss could give Iran what it wants.
